name: Restaurant Brands International Inc.

profile.description: Restaurant Brands International owns and franchises four quick-service brands: Tim Hortons, Burger King, Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen, and Firehouse Subs. It operates in more than 100 countries and has executive offices in Toronto and Miami [6]. TTM revenue through Q3 2026 was $9.78B (+5.5% YoY). In Q3 2026, system-wide sales grew 6.2% (International +9.0%) and global comparable sales rose 3.8%, led by Burger King US at +8.4% [1][3]. Joshua Kobza, previously RBI's CFO, CTO and COO, has been CEO since March 2023 [7].

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Recent change has come mainly through M&A and restructuring (adding Firehouse Subs as a fourth brand, then turning around Burger King US, whose comparable sales rose 8.4% in Q3 2026) rather than new products or business models [1][6]. AI Deployment (0/2): Our searches found no quantified AI products or AI-driven savings disclosed by RBI. Market Share (1/2): RBI's brands are major global QSR players with system-wide sales up 6.2% and International up 9.0% in Q3 2026, but the evidence shows them as large participants rather than share leaders [1]. Product Pipeline (0/2): Guidance centers on 8% organic adjusted operating income growth and unit development, not named next-generation offerings [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): RBI reports no R&D expense [3].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): RBI presents itself as a builder and franchisor of iconic restaurant brands, a generic, finance-led identity, and corporate messaging centers on system-wide sales and operating income growth [1][6]. Community Impact (0/2): Our searches did not find specific charitable program data. ESG coverage showed only shareholder activism over cage-free egg benchmarks (2023) and supply-chain deforestation (2018) [9]. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention data. Franchisee conflict at Tim Hortons ('Battle at Timmies') points to strained system relationships [10]. Insider Buying (0/2): FMP records zero open-market purchases and 63 open-market sales by insiders across Q4 2025-Q3 2026 [8].

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on all 10 dividend-sleeve metrics (12 weight units). Strengths: ROE of 39.6% (1.0), 5-year revenue CAGR of 13.7% (FY2020 $4.97B to FY2025 $9.43B, partly from consolidating acquired restaurants; 1.0), and a forward P/E of 16.6 (derived: $72.41 / blended FY2026-FY2027 consensus EPS of ~$4.35; 1.0) [3][4]. The dividend record is strong: 12 consecutive years paid since 2015 (1.0, 2x) and 11 consecutive annual increases, from $0.09 per quarter in 2015 to $0.65 in 2026 (1.0) [5]. The drags are D/E of 392% (0.0), a 76.5% payout ratio (0.39), and a 5-year dividend CAGR of 4.2% ($2.12 in 2021 to $2.60 in 2026; 0.70, 2x) [3][5]. TTM revenue growth of 5.5% scores 0.85 and the TTM net margin of 15.3% scores 0.77. Weighted sum 9.40/12 = 7.8, rounded to 8. Liquidity is about 2.9M shares/day x $72.41 (~$210M daily).

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): RBI sells physical food and beverages through about 30,000 restaurants, and AI cannot replace a burger, coffee, or a drive-thru visit, so core demand is protected [6]. AI mostly affects ordering, labor scheduling, and marketing, where it is a cost tool for franchisees rather than a substitute, though AI-driven delivery platforms could shift pricing power toward aggregators. AI Opportunity (0/1): RBI does not disclose AI-related revenue, and our searches found no quantified AI results [7].

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, RBI is a brand-holding company built by 3G Capital to optimize franchise economics, and its scorecard is system-wide sales growth, organic operating income growth, and cash returned ($1.3B in 2026 to date). CEO Josh Kobza's move to give the brands more autonomy and the reinvestment in Burger King US show some long-term thinking. But there is no Just Cause, franchisee relations have been contentious, and growth has come largely through acquisitions and leverage (D/E of 392%).

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): RBI's brands carry heritage (Tim Hortons as a Canadian institution, Burger King's flame-grilling), but the parent's stated purpose is building and franchising brands for growth, and leadership speaks in terms of comparable sales and adjusted operating income targets [1][6]. A purpose exists only at the brand level and does not drive RBI-level strategy.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Kobza is a long-tenured insider (CFO 2014-2018, CTO, COO, CEO since 2023), and one of his first priorities was to give the divisional brands more autonomy and cut centralized layers, a decentralizing move [7]. Against that, franchisee activism at Tim Hortons and the cost-focused culture associated with RBI's history limit trust to an adequate level [10].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Competitive framing is about comparable-sales outperformance and value wars against McDonald's, Wendy's and Starbucks. We found no evidence of management treating rivals as teachers [1].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): RBI has reshaped its model by adding Popeyes and Firehouse Subs, moving between refranchising and buying back restaurants to remodel (Burger King US), and taking control of some international master franchises. International system sales are growing 9% [1][6]. These are portfolio moves within the same franchisor model, not a cause-driven reinvention.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Management reinvested heavily in Burger King US remodels and operations despite near-term cost, and that investment now shows in +8.4% BK US comps in Q3 2026 [1]. It keeps paying a 76% payout dividend and returned $1.3B in 2026 to date while carrying 392% D/E, which favors shareholder distributions over balance-sheet resilience [1][3].

investment_thesis: RBI is executing well. Q3 2026 system-wide sales grew 6.2%, global comparable sales rose 3.8% with Burger King US at +8.4%, International sales grew 9.0%, and management reiterated 8% organic adjusted operating income growth for 2026 [1]. At $72.41 the stock trades near 16.6x forward earnings with a 3.6% yield, backed by 11 straight years of dividend increases (the quarterly rate rose to $0.65 in 2026), and consensus EPS climbs from about $4.04 in 2026 to $4.41 in 2027 [4][5].
thesis_continued: The bear case is leverage and quality of growth. D/E is 392%, net debt is about 4.9x EBITDA, tangible book value is negative (-$33/share), and the 76% payout ratio leaves limited room if comparable sales slow [3]. The 13.7% 5-year revenue CAGR overstates organic growth because it includes consolidating acquired restaurants. Franchisee tensions, heavy insider selling, and consumer value wars in U.S. QSR could pressure margins and the 4.2% dividend growth rate [5][8][10].
key_catalysts: Sustained Burger King US turnaround: Q3 2026 comparable sales of +8.4% could keep driving franchisee profitability and remodel momentum [1]
International expansion: 9.0% international system-wide sales growth gives a long runway for unit growth [1]
Delivering 8% organic adjusted operating income growth in 2026 supports continued dividend increases from the current $0.65 quarterly rate [1][5]
key_risks: Leverage: 392% D/E and ~4.9x net debt/EBITDA make RBI sensitive to refinancing rates and leave little cushion in a consumer downturn [3]
Dividend growth slowdown: the 76% payout ratio and 4.2% 5-year dividend CAGR leave limited headroom for faster increases [3][5]
Franchisee and consumer pressure: Tim Hortons franchisee disputes and a U.S. QSR value war could compress system margins [10]
